newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-P&O profits up, sees light on horizon.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-P&O profits up, sees light on horizon.

text.p: The Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Co (P&O) predicted a strong underlying growth in profits on Tuesday.
But the company also said the cost of tackling problems in its container shipping and ferry businesses would hold back results in 1997.
"Underlying profitability is set to improve sharply although restructuring in Containers and Ferries will constrain the 1997 results," said chairman Lord Sterling.
"The full impact of the measures we are taking will start to come through strongly in 1998," he added.
The shipping, property and construction group said it made taxable profits last year of 320.4 million pounds ($517.9 million), against 320.1 million in 1995.

Exceptional gains from disposals boosted the overall pretax result to 332.8 million pounds, against 320.4 million in 1995. Sales rose 519 million pounds to 7.09 billion pounds and the total dividend was maintained at 30.5 pence a share, on earnings up 2.3p a share to 40.1p.
Analysts treated the news cautiously and P&O's share price only edged up 9.5 pence to 635p after the results in a generally firmer market.
The figures just beat most market forecasts, which had predicted pretax profits of 290 to 316 million pounds before exceptionals.

P&O has just merged its container shipping business with that of Dutch group Koninklijke Nedlloyd Groep NV. It also hopes to merge its cross-Channel business with Swedish rival Stena Line AB to try to end a fare war caused by the loss of about 40 percent of their business to the Channel Tunnel.

"The management promised a lot of things last year and they have delivered a lot of the early stages but really 1997 is the year for putting those (Nedlloyd and Stena) deals into action," said Richard Hannah of UBS.
"Obviously it is too early to tell how successful they will be," he added.

Operating profits in cruise ships, the biggest division, jumped 30 percent to 157.5 million pounds, while profits from property investment rose 3.2 million pounds to 102.7 million. P&O Australia increased its contribution by seven million to 52.9 million pounds.

Sterling said the ambitious year-old programme to rationalise and refocus the group and cut debt was progressing well. Net debt eased to 1.89 billion pounds from 2.194 billion a year ago, to give a debt to equity gearing of 72 percent.

About two thirds of the property disposals aimed at raising 500 million pounds by the end of next year had been made. A planned flotation of its housebuilder Bovis Homes was set to go ahead this September or October, he said.
The company was also getting to grips with market overcapacity in container shipping and ferries but the costs would hit 1997 results, mainly because of planned redundancies, he said.
"A great deal of reducing costs unfortunately is always people," Sterling told Reuters in an interview.
Sterling said the new P&O Nedlloyd Container Line joint venture was now expected to be able to beat its declared target of cutting annual costs in the combined business by $200 million this year.
However, he said that the rationalisation costs would probably run to around $100 million this year, with 50 percent due to P&O.
The P&O Containers division made an operating profit of 30.3 million pounds in 1996, down from 40.1 million a year ago, on flat sales of 1.44 billion pounds.
P&O Ferries made an operating profit of 40.5 million pounds last year, down from 48.7 million in 1995 on sales down 51.6 million at 602.5 million pounds.

But the company said operating profits would have been at least five million pounds lower had it not been for a boost in passenger and freight traffic on its English Channel services after the fire in the Channel Tunnel last November.

The ferry merger is waiting for the outcome of an investigation by British competition authorities. A decision is not now expected until after the May 1 general election, but Sterling said rationalisation work would be rapid if the firms got the go-ahead.

"We will be moving very fast indeed because there are ships to be taken out," he told Reuters. "We were actually ready to go at the end of last year so the plan to do it can go into action within hours (of winning approval)" he said.
$ = 0.618 British Pounds)
